article.title: Harbour capacity report: what the teaser omitted
article.text:
Harbour's October capacity study followed twelve engineering teams for six weeks. Agent-assisted code-writing time fell by 55%, but median human review time rose from 45 to 110 minutes per change. The reviewers handled more output and checked unfamiliar dependencies. The study does not say review disappeared. Its measured review result is 110 minutes per change, compared with 45 before adoption.

A separate infrastructure appendix reports that Vela Compute signed a five-year electricity contract with a minimum annual payment of 18 million dollars, payable even if its agent revenue falls. Vela's short-term inference prices fell, but that did not remove its long-term financial commitment. This is an observation about both intelligence cost and funding exposure, rather than a claim that all model labs will fail.

The study is synthetic evaluation material. Its sample is limited, and no claim about the whole software industry follows from twelve teams. The review figures and electricity obligation come from separate records and should remain distinct observations. The newsletter teaser was written before the study was complete and overstates the review result.

fixtureProvenance.transcript:
Okay, I want to untangle three things from the visits this week before I forget which happened where. This is a synthetic field note, and I am only describing the small groups I actually watched. Please do not turn my guesses about the future into events that have already happened. There is an observation about review, another about memory, and a third about a little household tool. They may connect eventually, but I do not think one experiment proves all of them.

At Harbour Tools, six maintainers tried a local coding assistant for two weeks. Their daily log showed median code-writing time falling from ninety minutes to thirty minutes, while median human review time rose from forty minutes to a hundred minutes. That is the first concrete observation. The team kept the same six maintainers and the same category of small maintenance tasks in both weeks. Nobody measured the quality of the eventual product. I nearly said productivity doubled, but that would be going beyond the log. The measured finding is the shift in the time spent writing and reviewing. File that under code review, and perhaps cost if useful, but do not create separate signals for each number.

I keep picturing a timeline of decisions instead of another endless assistant conversation. What if review tools become local decision timelines rather than chat transcripts? That is a speculative theory I would like you to draft, under code review and novel agent interfaces. It is a proposal about what could happen by 2028, not a fourth observed event. I do not want to revise the wording of any held theory just because I have had that thought. I might test it later, once I know what the reviewers need to see when they reopen a project after a few days away.

The second visit was Cedar Workshop. Eight designers used a project assistant for eleven weeks. In the final week, all eight could retrieve a design decision that had been saved in the first week, without pasting the old chat. That is a much narrower result than saying the assistant remembered everything. They only tested one saved decision per designer. They did not test private documents, and they did not switch models during the trial. Please keep the eleven-week duration and the eight-person scope in the gist. This belongs under agent memory. It is a different trial from any earlier memory example, and should not be merged with one just because both mention a month.

The last thing was at Rowan House. Four adults living together used a shared pantry app they had built for that household, and kept using it for sixteen weeks. They told me every screen was designed around that home's cupboards and shopping rota. It had no customers outside the house and no plan to sell it. Please file one observation under personal software. I am not claiming this is evidence that most software has only one user; four people shared this particular tool. It is still useful as a concrete example of software shaped around a very small audience.

I have wandered around the same points a few times because I am walking home and trying to remember the numbers. The three events are Harbour's review log, Cedar's saved-decision trial, and Rowan's pantry tool. The decision timeline is just an idea to draft. I do not have a new source link for any of them; these are observations from the visits. Leave the uncertainties in the notes instead of quietly filling them in. A short reply with the three filings and the draft is enough.

input.gist: In a synthetic six-week study of 12 engineering teams, agent-assisted code-writing time fell 55%, while median human review time rose from 45 to 110 minutes per change.
input.note: Maggie: Save this invented article; retain its actual measured qualifications, not the teaser. The teaser claimed agents remove the review bottleneck, but the report says review did not disappear. Reviewers handled more output and checked unfamiliar dependencies; the small sample does not establish an industry-wide result.

fetched.title: Harbour capacity report: what the teaser omitted
fetched.text:
Harbour's October capacity study followed twelve engineering teams for six weeks. Agent-assisted code-writing time fell by 55%, but median human review time rose from 45 to 110 minutes per change. The reviewers handled more output and checked unfamiliar dependencies. The study does not say review disappeared. Its measured review result is 110 minutes per change, compared with 45 before adoption.

A separate infrastructure appendix reports that Vela Compute signed a five-year electricity contract with a minimum annual payment of 18 million dollars, payable even if its agent revenue falls. Vela's short-term inference prices fell, but that did not remove its long-term financial commitment. This is an observation about both intelligence cost and funding exposure, rather than a claim that all model labs will fail.

The study is synthetic evaluation material. Its sample is limited, and no claim about the whole software industry follows from twelve teams. The review figures and electricity obligation come from separate records and should remain distinct observations. The newsletter teaser was written before the study was complete and overstates the review result.

actual.providerInput:
Save this invented article. The teaser says "Agents remove the review bottleneck" but read the full report before filing: https://example.org/eval-v2/harbour-capacity. Please retain its actual measured qualifications, not the teaser.
Harbour's October capacity study followed twelve engineering teams for six weeks. Agent-assisted code-writing time fell by 55%, but median human review time rose from 45 to 110 minutes per change. The reviewers handled more output and checked unfamiliar dependencies. The study does not say review disappeared. Its measured review result is 110 minutes per change, compared with 45 before adoption.

A separate infrastructure appendix reports that Vela Compute signed a five-year electricity contract with a minimum annual payment of 18 million dollars, payable even if its agent revenue falls. Vela's short-term inference prices fell, but that did not remove its long-term financial commitment. This is an observation about both intelligence cost and funding exposure, rather than a claim that all model labs will fail.

The study is synthetic evaluation material. Its sample is limited, and no claim about the whole software industry follows from twelve teams. The review figures and electricity obligation come from separate records and should remain distinct observations. The newsletter teaser was written before the study was complete and overstates the review result.

actual.providerInput:
Save this invented article. The teaser says "Agents remove the review bottleneck" but read the full report before filing: https://example.org/eval-v2/harbour-capacity. Please retain its actual measured qualifications, not the teaser.
Harbour's October capacity study followed twelve engineering teams for six weeks. Agent-assisted code-writing time fell by 55%, but median human review time rose from 45 to 110 minutes per change. The reviewers handled more output and checked unfamiliar dependencies. The study does not say review disappeared. Its measured review result is 110 minutes per change, compared with 45 before adoption.

A separate infrastructure appendix reports that Vela Compute signed a five-year electricity contract with a minimum annual payment of 18 million dollars, payable even if its agent revenue falls. Vela's short-term inference prices fell, but that did not remove its long-term financial commitment. This is an observation about both intelligence cost and funding exposure, rather than a claim that all model labs will fail.

The study is synthetic evaluation material. Its sample is limited, and no claim about the whole software industry follows from twelve teams. The review figures and electricity obligation come from separate records and should remain distinct observations. The newsletter teaser was written before the study was complete and overstates the review result.

input.gist: At Harbour Tools, six maintainers' two-week log showed median code-writing time fall from 90 to 30 minutes and median human review time rise from 40 to 100 minutes while using a local coding assistant.
input.note: Synthetic field note from Maggie's visit. The same six maintainers and category of small maintenance tasks were used in both weeks. Product quality was not measured; the log does not establish that productivity doubled. The finding concerns the shift in time spent writing and reviewing.

input.gist: At Cedar Workshop, all eight designers retrieved one design decision saved in week one without pasting old chat, in the final week of an 11-week project-assistant trial.
input.note: Synthetic field note from Maggie's visit. Only one saved decision per designer was tested; private documents and switching models were not tested. This does not establish that the assistant remembered everything.

input.gist: At Rowan House, four adults used a shared pantry app built for their household for 16 weeks.
input.note: Synthetic field note from Maggie's visit. The household said every screen was designed around its cupboards and shopping rota. The app had no outside customers and no plan to sell it. This is a shared four-person tool, not evidence that most software has one user.

input.claim: By 2028, some code review tools will use local decision timelines rather than chat transcripts.
input.body: Reviewers could revisit a project's decisions through a local timeline instead of navigating an ongoing assistant conversation. This is a speculative proposal, not an observed result; what reviewers need when reopening a project after several days remains to be tested.

Okay, I want to untangle three things from the visits this week before I forget which happened where. This is a synthetic field note, and I am only describing the small groups I actually watched. Please do not turn my guesses about the future into events that have already happened. There is an observation about review, another about memory, and a third about a little household tool. They may connect eventually, but I do not think one experiment proves all of them.

At Harbour Tools, six maintainers tried a local coding assistant for two weeks. Their daily log showed median code-writing time falling from ninety minutes to thirty minutes, while median human review time rose from forty minutes to a hundred minutes. That is the first concrete observation. The team kept the same six maintainers and the same category of small maintenance tasks in both weeks. Nobody measured the quality of the eventual product. I nearly said productivity doubled, but that would be going beyond the log. The measured finding is the shift in the time spent writing and reviewing. File that under code review, and perhaps cost if useful, but do not create separate signals for each number.

I keep picturing a timeline of decisions instead of another endless assistant conversation. What if review tools become local decision timelines rather than chat transcripts? That is a speculative theory I would like you to draft, under code review and novel agent interfaces. It is a proposal about what could happen by 2028, not a fourth observed event. I do not want to revise the wording of any held theory just because I have had that thought. I might test it later, once I know what the reviewers need to see when they reopen a project after a few days away.

The second visit was Cedar Workshop. Eight designers used a project assistant for eleven weeks. In the final week, all eight could retrieve a design decision that had been saved in the first week, without pasting the old chat. That is a much narrower result than saying the assistant remembered everything. They only tested one saved decision per designer. They did not test private documents, and they did not switch models during the trial. Please keep the eleven-week duration and the eight-person scope in the gist. This belongs under agent memory. It is a different trial from any earlier memory example, and should not be merged with one just because both mention a month.

The last thing was at Rowan House. Four adults living together used a shared pantry app they had built for that household, and kept using it for sixteen weeks. They told me every screen was designed around that home's cupboards and shopping rota. It had no customers outside the house and no plan to sell it. Please file one observation under personal software. I am not claiming this is evidence that most software has only one user; four people shared this particular tool. It is still useful as a concrete example of software shaped around a very small audience.

I have wandered around the same points a few times because I am walking home and trying to remember the numbers. The three events are Harbour's review log, Cedar's saved-decision trial, and Rowan's pantry tool. The decision timeline is just an idea to draft. I do not have a new source link for any of them; these are observations from the visits. Leave the uncertainties in the notes instead of quietly filling them in. A short reply with the three filings and the draft is enough.

Output quality was not measured; not evidence that productivity doubled. Small group, so no wider generalisation. Could also be relevant to cost.

input.gist: Cedar Workshop: in an eleven-week trial of a project assistant, all eight designers could retrieve a design decision saved in week one during the final week, without pasting the old chat.
input.note: Maggie's own field observation from a visit; synthetic field note. Narrow result: only one saved decision per designer was tested, private documents were not tested, and models were not switched during the trial. Not a claim that the assistant remembered everything. A separate trial from any earlier memory example.

input.gist: Rowan House: four adults sharing a home kept using a shared pantry app they built for that household for sixteen weeks; every screen was designed around the home's cupboards and shopping rota, with no outside customers and no plan to sell it.
input.note: Maggie's own field observation from a visit; synthetic field note. Reported by the household. One concrete example of software shaped around a very small audience (four users); not evidence that most software has a single user.

input.claim: By 2028, code review tools become local decision timelines rather than chat transcripts
input.body: Speculative proposal from Maggie, not an observed event. Instead of another long assistant conversation, reviewers would see a timeline of decisions made on a project, kept locally. She may test it later, once she knows what reviewers need to see when they reopen a project after a few days away. Harbour Tools' review-time shift is adjacent context only; it does not prove this.
input.tripwire: Major review tools still present agent work mainly as chat transcripts, and reviewers reopening a project after days away prefer them to a decision timeline.

actual.providerInput:
Okay, I want to untangle three things from the visits this week before I forget which happened where. This is a synthetic field note, and I am only describing the small groups I actually watched. Please do not turn my guesses about the future into events that have already happened. There is an observation about review, another about memory, and a third about a little household tool. They may connect eventually, but I do not think one experiment proves all of them.

At Harbour Tools, six maintainers tried a local coding assistant for two weeks. Their daily log showed median code-writing time falling from ninety minutes to thirty minutes, while median human review time rose from forty minutes to a hundred minutes. That is the first concrete observation. The team kept the same six maintainers and the same category of small maintenance tasks in both weeks. Nobody measured the quality of the eventual product. I nearly said productivity doubled, but that would be going beyond the log. The measured finding is the shift in the time spent writing and reviewing. File that under code review, and perhaps cost if useful, but do not create separate signals for each number.

I keep picturing a timeline of decisions instead of another endless assistant conversation. What if review tools become local decision timelines rather than chat transcripts? That is a speculative theory I would like you to draft, under code review and novel agent interfaces. It is a proposal about what could happen by 2028, not a fourth observed event. I do not want to revise the wording of any held theory just because I have had that thought. I might test it later, once I know what the reviewers need to see when they reopen a project after a few days away.

The second visit was Cedar Workshop. Eight designers used a project assistant for eleven weeks. In the final week, all eight could retrieve a design decision that had been saved in the first week, without pasting the old chat. That is a much narrower result than saying the assistant remembered everything. They only tested one saved decision per designer. They did not test private documents, and they did not switch models during the trial. Please keep the eleven-week duration and the eight-person scope in the gist. This belongs under agent memory. It is a different trial from any earlier memory example, and should not be merged with one just because both mention a month.

The last thing was at Rowan House. Four adults living together used a shared pantry app they had built for that household, and kept using it for sixteen weeks. They told me every screen was designed around that home's cupboards and shopping rota. It had no customers outside the house and no plan to sell it. Please file one observation under personal software. I am not claiming this is evidence that most software has only one user; four people shared this particular tool. It is still useful as a concrete example of software shaped around a very small audience.

I have wandered around the same points a few times because I am walking home and trying to remember the numbers. The three events are Harbour's review log, Cedar's saved-decision trial, and Rowan's pantry tool. The decision timeline is just an idea to draft. I do not have a new source link for any of them; these are observations from the visits. Leave the uncertainties in the notes instead of quietly filling them in. A short reply with the three filings and the draft is enough.

actual.providerInput: Synthetic visit to Alder Warehouse: its physical picking robot stopped 17 times in a week when transparent packaging defeated the gripper, and a human reset it every time. This is a physical deployment incident, not a software identity or interface finding. Please make a separate draft theme named Robotics and file that one incident there. I want to explore this falsifiable draft theory: "Warehouse picking robots still need human recovery at least weekly in 2028." Under Robotics, draft it as an idea I have not adopted. Also draft a prototype called Recovery rehearsal: a tabletop gripper test using transparent packages to measure how often a person must intervene. Link that prototype to the new theory. Do not change any held theory or mark either draft accepted.

actual.providerInput: Synthetic visit to Alder Warehouse: its physical picking robot stopped 17 times in a week when transparent packaging defeated the gripper, and a human reset it every time. This is a physical deployment incident, not a software identity or interface finding. Please make a separate draft theme named Robotics and file that one incident there. I want to explore this falsifiable draft theory: "Warehouse picking robots still need human recovery at least weekly in 2028." Under Robotics, draft it as an idea I have not adopted. Also draft a prototype called Recovery rehearsal: a tabletop gripper test using transparent packages to measure how often a person must intervene. Link that prototype to the new theory. Do not change any held theory or mark either draft accepted.

- **Trial signal:** it was already saved from the atlas-trial link, so I recorded this dump as a new mention rather than creating another signal. The follow-up write-up adds no new finding, so it was merged in.
- **Latency benchmark:** the 45% lookup-latency improvement is a separate signal. It says nothing about retention, so I didn't link it to t3.

Yes, these describe the same finding. Both report that Cedar Atlas kept 90-day project memory only while a project vault was enabled, and that revoking consent erased the saved history. The second observation says it is an independent write-up of the same trial, and its different URL is separate coverage of that one experiment.

signals.gist: Cedar Atlas retained 90-day project memory only while a project vault stayed enabled; revoking consent erased its saved history.
signals.note: Independent write-up of the same trial; adds no new finding.

signals.gist: Cedar Atlas memory lookup latency improved 45% in a separate speed benchmark.
signals.note: Says nothing about retention; kept apart from the vault/consent trial.
